segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is hard, gritty/crunchy (ざくざく), as if frozen, tasteless/nasty (不味). Period poor-cooking/storage detail. Keep physical and uninterpreted; do not make it symbolize poverty or turn causality explicit (potato = vision). English must keep teeth, coldness, lack of taste without ennobling or explaining.

幻のような絵, 淡暗い光り, 物静か — picture stays a picture seen by the eye, not a dream entered or doctrine concluded. Do not translate 絵 as vision/scene/world, 幻 as hallucination/dream, or upgrade dimness into mysticism.

懐かしみ (natsukashimi), 許し, 安らかさ, 安息 — repeated network. Natsukashimi is fond remembrance/longing, not nostalgia in modern English sense and not forgiveness; 許し is pardon/forgiveness. Keep same English words each time; do not expand into explanations or merge them.

あの日, 永久に夜のような安息 — that day / night-like rest. Could imply death, old age, eternity, judgement. Text leaves open. Keep literal 'that day' and 'rest like night'; do not name heaven, death, afterlife, or judgement day.

Child explicitly girl but called 坊や (Bōya, literally boy). Period affectionate generic for baby. Keep 'Bōya' (romanised, explained in margin once) rather than 'boy/son/little one' which either misgenders or erases the wrinkle, and do not invent a name.

卓《テーブル》, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》 — Taishō literary with old kana and ruby glosses. Table is Western-style table under bare bulb; aluminium pot, earthen teapot, beef/onion/carrot/potato mark pauvre modernity. Render plainly without exoticizing or modernizing; ruby shows reading, not emphasis.

motifs.english: Keep one short word: 'storm'. Same noun in p1 announcement, p8 unheard, p19 heard alone, p38 whisper. Do not vary to tempest/gale or swell last line into symbol.
motifs.why: Acoustic frame that opens, disappears, and closes the story. Its return marks contraction back to present.

motifs.english: Keep 'smile' for 微笑/ほほえみ/笑み/笑い throughout, even where English would vary to grin/laugh. Child's noise vs parents' helpless smiling is the first-movement music.
motifs.why: Deliberate chain linking domestic laughter to the still smiling of the three figures; varying breaks the link.

motifs.english: Keep 'eyes / gaze' stable. 瞳 for soft deep looking, 眼 for lifted/strained looking. Do not upgrade to stare/gaze shifting.
motifs.why: Attention is the story's action: parents gaze at child, mother gazes far, vision is seen in eye's bottom.

motifs.english: Keep 'far / far off / far heart' literally, even repetitively. Distance becomes a place, not a metaphor to tidy.
motifs.why: Ordinary diction of distance carries the slide out of time; paraphrase would rationalize it.

motifs.english: Keep 'all / everything' for すべて/総て. Flat and total, not 'whole world' or 'life'.
motifs.why: Totalizing word that lets vision claim everything (good/evil/sorrow/joy) without showing any event.

motifs.english: Keep 'long' for ながい/永く. Do not vary to endless/eternal except where Japanese says 絶えることなく/永久に.
motifs.why: Three years feel long; story told is long; suffering after is long. Repetition makes 'only three years' land.

motifs.english: Keep 'quiet/still/silent' family together: 静か, 黙って, 黙る, 静まりかへった. Silence set against noise and against husband's 'why are you silent?'
motifs.why: Second half is defined by mother's silence against first-half racket; husband's repeated question marks it.

motifs.english: Keep 'tiredness / weary' for 疲れ/だるそう/打沈んだ. Physical, shared, young yet exhausted; do not pathologize.
motifs.why: Establishes poverty of strength without wrinkles; motivates but does not explain vision.

motifs.english: Keep fixed trio: 'fond remembrance (natsukashimi) and forgiveness and peace'. Gloss natsukashimi once in margin; thereafter same words. 'That day' stays 'that day'.
motifs.motif: fond remembrance, forgiveness, peace / night-like rest
motifs.why: Vision's whole content is these nouns; any elegant variation turns summary into doctrine.

motifs.english: Keep wife's exact refrain 'only three years / barely three years' (p14, p22, p27) and husband's echo 'only two years past' (p25, p28). Do not improve her inarticulacy.
motifs.motif: only three years; just a little longer; let's work
motifs.why: Contraction back to ordinary time and unexalted endurance; mother's eloquence must stay limited to this.

narration.english_tense: Simple past throughout as default. Keep explanatory past (it was, it was that) for p2-p4 scene-setting and for gnomic vision summary p17; do not switch vision to present timeless or dialogue to present.
narration.frame: One supper in a small room under a dark bulb, storm outside. Narration begins external and comic-crowded, drifts with mother without scene-break, contracts to table-clearing and whispered storm.
narration.narrator: Third-person external narrator, initially distanced (親子, 男, 女), imperceptibly becoming mother's interior focalization from p10-p11 onward. No italics, no dream-marking, no psychologizing verbs; hedges (いつか, ふと, いつとなく, なにか, ように) and explanatory endings (であった, のであった, のだった) keep reverie in same grammar as table.
narration.tense_habits: Japanese past/explanatory (であった, のであった, のだった) for both outer fact and inner summary; progressive/distal forms (〜しつつ, 〜ようとしてゐる, 〜てゐた) for ongoing supper vs completed drift. Hedged perception verbs, not marked thought.
timeline: p1-p9: crowded comic supper — baby stands holding table, bangs spoon, parents sweep everything below table, forget storm in racket
p10-p11: trigger — mother serves beef/onion/carrot/potato from blue pot, tastes hard gritty tasteless potato, falls vaguely silent
p12-p18: expansion — three married years feel lifelong, sufferings recalled dreamlike, phantom-like picture of three telling endless story, night-like rest ahead
p19-p32: return punctured by dialogue — husband twice 'why are you silent?', wife can only say 'only three years', husband answers 'two years past, baby will walk, a little longer', feeding resumes
p33-p38: close — chopsticks laid down, nursing, clear table sleep early tomorrow, child asleep at breast, stillness, husband stands whispering storm

body.say: This bible keeps the supper crowded and the vision dim: repeat smile, eyes, far, all, long, quiet, tiredness, and the fixed trio of fond remembrance/forgiveness/peace in plain past-tense English, leave that day and the three figures unidentified, leave Bōya as Bōya, and let the storm frame open and shut without swelling.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse; margin only where sentence cannot give reader the thing: Bōya (affectionate address for baby despite girl child), aluminium pot / beef-pot supper as poverty-modernity, 懐かしみ gloss once, old-kana ruby convention. Never annotate what context supplies or explain that day.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taishō literary but not quaint: soft, slightly formal, accumulative long sentences with repetitions, then short dialogue punctures. Keep drift in same diction as table; no italics for thought, no vividness upgrade for vision, no sentimentality for baby, no consolation conclusion. Husband's practical hope stands equal to vision.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No personal names in text. Use 'the man / the young father', 'the woman / the mother', 'the child / the baby' as Japanese does; do not normalize to husband/wife/father/mother throughout. Keep 'Bōya' for 坊や as address with one margin note; do not translate to boy/son/baby.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Bōya only, in romanisation with macron-less plain form. All else in English: Sensei-type retention does not apply (no 先生). Foods, vessels (rice, aluminium pot, earthen teapot, tea-bowl) in plain English.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for direct speech and ひとりで独言. In English use double quotation marks for spoken lines (p7, p21-p35, p38 whisper). Husband's どうして黙ってるの twice must read as same question. Do not join dialogue to narration or split drift sentences to make logic clearer.
style_sheet.register: Clean, soft, slightly formal past-tense English. Poverty plain without ennoblement; comedy bodily without cuteness; abstraction flat without elegance. Repeat words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese varies.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby in source (卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》) shows reading; render as normal English ('table', 'shrewd', 'smile') with no italics. No italics for vision or thought. Italics only for Bōya as foreign address on first use if house style requires, then roman.

head.say:
Pick: Option 0.

Both readers name the same crux: the bad potato opens, without explanation, a view of the present supper from beyond a whole life, and the story depends on that expansion and its plain contraction to three years and tomorrow's work. Option 1's repetition and unbroken domestic surface are the mechanism of that movement, already described in Option 0's frame, recurrences, and diction of distance, not a separate crux. Option 0 therefore stands as the house reading because it holds trigger, vision, and return in the single movement by which the text stands or falls.

House log: The two independent crux statements were judged to name the same movement, and Option 0 was adopted as the house reading.

crux.for_the_english: Do not label it — not 'she imagined heaven', 'she dreamed', 'she thought of death'. Keep the modal, unresolved terms ('that day', 'would', 'seemed', 'as if'), let the vision arrive and recede unexplained, and keep it visually still rather than turning it into narrative action.
crux.point: The bad potato turns an ordinary supper into life seen from beyond its end, and that vision must stay unexplained.
crux.why: Nothing dramatic happens: in p11–13 the potato is inexplicably hard, 'frozen', tasteless, and its 'unconnected cold badness' detaches the young mother from the room. She feels suddenly old, remembers the three married years as if from far away — suffering already 'like a dream' (p13) — then sees, p16–18, three motionless figures in dim light telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy are all spoken of, yet wrapped only in 'nostalgia and forgiveness' and deep rest, 'like night'. In p20 she repeats the turn as certainty: 'that day exists', after long life, long sorrow. The story stands on this not being reduced to a cause: not simply fatigue, not a stated premonition of death, not religious consolation, not a daydream about old age. It is the present moment already viewed from after time has passed over it (p17: life will pass, and only on that passed day does everything change to nostalgia and forgiveness).

crux.for_the_english: Resist rationalisation, expansion and synonym-variation (Berman's tidyings). Keep long cumulative sentences where the Japanese accumulates, repeat the same English words for the same Japanese ones — quiet, lonely, far, rest/peace, nostalgic/dear, smile, dream — even where elegant English would vary them, and keep dialogue plain and slightly unfinished ('It's only been... hasn't it', 'just a little longer').
crux.point: The incantatory repetition and unbroken domestic surface are how three years become a lifetime; varied, tightened prose would make the vision an inserted purple passage instead of a change of distance.
crux.why: The text works by recurrence, not event: storm heard at start, forgotten in the child's noise (p8, p19, p38), people repeatedly 'young' yet exhausted (p2–3 against p13–14: barely three years, yet she feels wholly aged), words circling — 静か, 淋しい, 遠い, 安らかさ, なつかしみ, 許し, 微笑, 夢 — across both the noisy supper and the silent vision, so the vision feels like the same room seen from far off rather than another world. Sentences also drift: dropped subjects, tense loosening, だろう / やうだ speculation, and dialogue that resolves nothing except 'let us work', 'clear up', 'get up early tomorrow' (p34–36).

second.say: The translation stands or falls on keeping the mother's vision in p16–20 ambiguous and on letting repetition, not event, stretch three years into a lifetime.
second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from elsewhere in Shiraki's work or contemporary reception that the 'day' is a specific, named doctrine (e.g. an explicit Christian afterlife or Buddhist rite she elsewhere names) would justify one clarifying note; nothing in this text names it, so any such label here would be invention.

body.why: This 38-paragraph short story is a single continuous supper scene of about 3,400 characters with no chapters or major breaks, so it is best judged whole as one part.

crux.for_the_english: So: keep the trigger physical and uninterpreted. The potato is hard — “as if frozen”, gritty between her teeth, tasteless — and the distance it opens in her is rendered in the narration's ordinary diction of distance itself (“far”, “far off”, “far heart”, “rate”, repeated until it becomes a place). Do not name what she sees: not heaven, not death, not her own old age, not a judgement day, though it has something of all of them. “あの日” is only “that day”. The picture must stay a picture — 幻のような絵, “a picture like a phantom”, something her eye sees, not a doctrine she arrives at. An English version that upgrades the vision into consolation — that lets her (or the narrator) conclude anything — has written a religious tract over a story about a bad potato. Likewise keep the return unexalted: “もう少しの間だ” — “just a little longer” — nursing the child, clearing the table, getting up early tomorrow. The vision does not solve the poverty. It sits next to it, and the story ends not on it but on a man standing still, whispering, 「嵐だな」 — “a storm”. That bare last line is the frame closing: the storm announced in p1, unheard through the child's noise in p8, heard by her alone inside her silence in p19, and finally heard by everyone in the quiet of p37–38. Keep it exactly that plain and that short; do not let it swell into a symbol at the last moment.
crux.point: "The crux is the mother's mid-mouthful slide out of time. For five paragraphs this is a warm, crowded, slightly comic supper: a fat baby girl just able to stand by holding the table, banging a spoon, everything swept out of her reach, two young parents — not a wrinkle on either face, but a deep, drowsy tiredness already in his hollowed eyes and her fine shoulders — laughing helplessly and forgetting, in the racket, even to hear the storm outside. Then, in p10–p11, the mother puts a potato in her mouth. It is hard, gritty, as if frozen, thoroughly nasty. She says nothing. And the prose, without any marker of a scene-change, drifts with her: the three years since her marriage stretch until she feels she has lived a whole long life and grown quite old; the sufferings of those three years come back “dreamlike”, and she is suddenly seeing, from very far away, a dim picture (絵) of three people with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, joy — is told, while nobody moves, nobody is disturbed, and all of it is wrapped in 懐かしみ (natsukashimi, fond remembrance) and 許し (forgiveness) and a deep peace like the night's. The story stands or falls on whether the English lets that expansion happen inside an ordinary sentence at an ordinary table, and then lets it contract again to “only three years” (p14, p22, p27) and to work tomorrow."
crux.why: Everything else in the text serves that one movement. The frame is built for it: storm heard / storm unheard / storm heard again. The child's noise in the first movement is not decoration — it is what the world sounds like from inside a life being lived at full stretch, and the mother's silence in the second half is set against her husband's repeated, puzzled 「どうして黙ってるの」 (“why are you so quiet?”, p19, p21) precisely because he cannot follow her where she has gone. And the vision's content is all summary and no event: nothing is shown happening, only everything having already happened and turned, in the telling, into fondness and pardon. If the English makes the vision vivid, specific or dramatic, the ratio inverts and it becomes a fantasy interrupting a domestic sketch, rather than the domestic sketch briefly seen from the far side of a whole life.

open_questions.question: Who are the three people in dim picture? Family aged, themselves in afterlife, humanity generic? Text keeps three quiet people, heads together. Don't identify.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If identified as family in old age/heaven, vision becomes specific consolation and loses universality/ambiguity.

open_questions.question: "That day" when all becomes nostalgia/forgiveness - death, old age, far future, eternity before night-like rest? Keep literal that day/night-like rest unresolved.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Naming death/heaven clarifies author's deliberate vagueness and changes theology/tone.

open_questions.question: Baby explicitly girl in p2, yet parents call her Bōya (boy/baby lad). Keep Bōya as affectionate generic 'baby/little one' without correcting gender or inventing name?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Correcting to 'little girl' erases period colloquial address; transliterating unexplained confuses.

open_questions.question: Potato: frozen-like hard gritty undercooked potato - literal poor cooking/storage period detail, not metaphor invented. Keep texture words close.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Symbolising potato destroys crux trigger's ordinariness.

body.reading: The crux must stay first in drafting. Beyond it, notice the narration's slide: begins outside ('a parent and child', 'the man', 'the woman') and imperceptibly becomes the mother's interior in same past-tense explanatory endings (de atta / no datta) and same 'as if', 'somehow', 'before she knew it' hedges. No italics, dreams marked, or psychologising verbs should separate reverie. Long sentences accumulate repetitions - smile (hohoemi), eyes/gaze, quiet/still, dream, all/everything (subete), long (nagai), far - then dialogue punctures with short exchanges. Repeat English words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese does. Register Taishō literary with old kana but not quaint: clean, soft, slightly formal English, poverty plain (rice, aluminium pot, beef onion carrot potato) without ennobling supper. Parents unnamed, young yet exhausted; child noisy bodily comedy prevents sentimentality. Husband's practical hope ('little one will soon walk', 'let's work') not lesser than vision. Fluent risks: rationalising potato-to-vision causality, clarifying 'that day', expanding abstract nouns into explanations, destroying rhythm by splitting drift or joining dialogue, impoverishing subete/nagai/far repetitions, making mother eloquent - she can say almost nothing, repeatedly 'only three years', and husband misunderstands kindly.
body.say: I can't settle identity of three figures or nature of that day from text; that's intentional ambiguity, not gap to fill. Also Bōya for girl child likely generic affectionate address in period, but keep visible as choice/fork.

voice_takes.label: Quiet drift (recommended)
voice_takes.line: "叙述は温かい同室の声から、区切りなく母の遠い心へ滑る" — narration slides without break from warm room to mother's far heart. Clean slightly formal prose, long looping sentences, repeated plain words; parents young plainspoken, husband blunt warm ('sa da naa' as soft 'that's so'), mother halting almost monosyllabic; wrong: lyrical uplift, heaven language, modern therapy idiom, cute baby-talk.

voice_takes.label: Plainer and drier
voice_takes.line: Shorter English sentences, abstract nouns kept bare (fondness, forgiveness, peace) without softening, dialogue working-plain. Risk: vision reads stark/fatalistic rather than tender.

voice_takes.label: Slightly period-formal
voice_takes.line: More formal diction and slower cadence matching 1917 literary surface, parents courteous-distanced. Risk: archaism makes poverty picturesque and mother remote, wrong if it sounds translated-old rather than young.

revision.english: Outside the door, darkened before they knew it, there was the sound of hard wind and rain. A storm.

The parent and child had gathered at the table under the dim electric light hanging close to the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. The father and the mother were both still truly young. And the child was a plump little girl, just able to stand by holding to the table.
notes: くりくりと肥ってる: kuri-kuri suggests roundness and plumpness rather than curly hair; rendered as plump to keep the bodily comedy plain.

revision.english: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kindly eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was to be seen a weary colour of tiredness. And in the colour of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was to be seen a still deeper, sunken tiredness, and a drowsy peace.
The day had ended. The sorrow and the suffering of that day were about to flow into the peace of the night. And they smiled in silence and fixed their eyes on all of the child.
notes: その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ kept as all of the child to preserve the subete repetition rather than smoothing to everything about her.

revision.english: Standing unsteadily, the child was trying with fat, round, ball-short hands to stir everything on the table, leaving not a moment's gap, and far too fast. So, smiling, they put everything, the tea-bowls and the earthen teapot and the aluminium pot, under the table. On the table there remained only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
notes: Tableware kept plain as poverty-modernity detail without gloss; smiling repeats the hohoemi chain.

revision.english: But the child gave a noisy cry full of small joy and banged the spoon and the plate down upon the table.

"You won't listen, will you." The young father gazed steadily at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with their rather dark, long lashes, moving nimbly and shrewdly without a pause, as if at a loss what to do, and then with a smile over his whole face, pinching lightly with his finger the child's round, thrust-out cheek, he took a large tea-bowl as if groping for it from under the table and put it in her hand.
notes: 'Her hand' is the child's hand: the Japanese pronoun here gives the large tea-bowl to the child, not to the mother. I kept 'her' because father and child are the only figures in the sentence.

revision.english: She served the hot, freshly cooked rice, with its white steam rising thick, from the pot and handed it to him. And her own young, large eyes, too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for a moment, lovely as a little bird. And as if unable to bear it, murmuring within her mouth, wondering whatever was the matter with this child, with a look of finding her so dear there was nothing to be done about it, she said firmly, "Bōya," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And as if having forgotten everything, the three smiled at one another as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle and with the smile and gladness welling up of itself on top of it. And in the clatter and noise, they did not hear the sound of the wind and rain.
notes: I keep Bōya in roman letters for 坊や: the child has been stated to be a girl, but the mother calls to her with this affectionate address. 'Boy' or a name would mislead.

revision.english: The young father kept his red, big hand spread busily over the table. And his eyes, holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, as he steadied the child he put a little food into that small red mouth. In between, hastily opening his own big mouth, he pushed rice into it.

The mother, silent with bowed head close by the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onion, the carrot and potato stewed in the deep blue pot. And about to say something, she put into her mouth a potato stewed sweet and soft, and looked at the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and gazed vacantly at a far place.

The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty between the teeth, as if it had frozen, and thoroughly nasty. As if startled, she said nothing and bit it again with her front teeth, but her heart had already, before she knew it, bowed down lonely.
notes: Kept texture close to the Japanese: hard, gritty, as if frozen, nasty, with front teeth, without making it explain the drift that follows.

revision.english: She recalled the suffering and sorrow and tiredness of each day. And the tasteless, indifferent, cold nastiness of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow-filled, real life since her marriage.
notes: Kept 'far-removed heart' literal as the ordinary diction of distance that carries the slide.

revision.english: And it seemed to her like a life that had gone on far too long. She found herself thinking, all at once, as if she had grown quite old. And of days filled with quiet tears, and of days threatened and spent in fear for material things, and of each and every day grieved and suffered through sickness, her far heart was quietly remembering. Yet to her remembering now, all of it was like a dream. Suffering and sorrow, too, were like a fond dream.
notes: 'For material things' keeps busshitsu literal; I take it as want and money pressure but did not replace it. 'Fond dream' keeps natsukashii in plain English, ahead of the natsukashimi trio, without turning it into nostalgia.

revision.english: And when she thought, it was no more than barely three years of life since her marriage.
She gazed vacantly far off, as if her attention had been caught by something before she knew it. Her quiet heart was, before she knew it, seeing a picture like a phantom.
notes: Kept e as 'picture' and maboroshi no you na as 'like a phantom', not vision or dream, so it stays something seen by the eye.

revision.english: It was in a dim, faint light, and, quiet like that light, three people drawing together with their heads together telling a long story. That story seemed to go on between them, so long and without ceasing. And in that story all seemed to be told, all the good and evil of the world, sorrow and suffering and anger and anguish, and joy, all of it. Yet those who spoke and those who listened only went on quietly and peacefully smiling, and they did not move at all. With their heads inclined and their eyes lowered, only quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to wrap them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
notes: Kept the three people unidentified and the picture a picture: no heaven, death or judgement added. Chose plain 'fond remembrance' for natsukashimi and 'forgiveness' for yurushi, and kept smile, all, long and quiet repeated as in the Japanese.

revision.english: All things of the world, a life, would pass. And only on that day, when it had passed, would all, all things, turn to fond remembrance and forgiveness. And at that time they would be before a rest like night, forever.
notes: Left 'that day' and 'a rest like night, forever' literal and unresolved; no consolation or doctrine concluded. Kept 'all, all things' and the same 'fond remembrance and forgiveness' as p16.

revision.english: The far picture was mirrored darkly and quietly in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely peace, that picture was to be seen. Young as she was, she sighed a lonely, secret sigh by herself, and glanced at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and the child, and remained silent.
notes: Kept 'far', 'eyes', 'lonely' and 'quiet' repeated as distance-words, and 'remained silent' to hold the silence against the earlier noise.

revision.english: "Why are you so quiet?" the man said, looking at the woman's face in puzzlement. She hurriedly tried to say something, but unable to say anything all at once she fell silent, and her eyes again ran far off. And she saw the picture like a phantom again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.
notes: Japanese has doushite here and naze in p21 for the same repeated question; I have kept the English identical.

revision.english: Yes. That day was there. The day when all would turn to fond remembrance and forgiveness and peace was there. After a long life, and after a long sorrow, and after a long suffering, on the day after all of that, that peaceful day of fond remembrance and forgiveness was there. What was the suffering or sorrow of each single day. What was the tiredness or trouble of each single day. Before she knew it she had a smile on her face.
notes: Kept that day unresolved and repeated long, all, and smile as in the Japanese.

revision.english:
"Why are you so quiet?" the man spoke to her again.

She raised her head as if startled and, smiling fondly, said as if asking him too to remember many things, even the happy things from before their marriage, "Really only a little time has passed since we were married, hasn't it."
notes: Grouped as one item because p21 breaks off in the middle of her action into the speech in p22, with p23 as its close.

revision.english: "That's so," the man too raised his eyes and said.
"It is only three years, isn't it. And yet you and I have been through a great deal."
notes: Kept only three years in plain words for the return to ordinary time.

revision.english: "Truly." She lowered her eyes again to try to look at that picture. But at once, "But it is still only three years, you know," she said, her eyes shining as if she must tell him of some great hope, though she herself did not know what it was.
notes: Grouped as one item because p26 breaks off into the speech in p27. Kept only three years in the wife's same plain refrain and left the great hope unexplained.

revision.english: "That's so. Though day by day we are tired and troubled and made to suffer by all sorts of things, two years are already past. In a little while Bōya will be walking."
notes: Kept Bōya in romanisation. The child is stated to be a girl in p2, but the parents address her as Bōya; I keep the address rather than translating it as boy or little one.

revision.english: The man looked at the child standing with the spoon in its hand as if with nothing to do. She at once called out gladly in a loud voice, "Bōya!" and at the same moment the child gave a loud cry and, looking at its mother's face, banged the spoon upon the table, "Uma-uma-uma-uma."
notes: p29-p31 form one continuous action in the Japanese and are joined here. Kept uma-uma as mere babble, not as yummy or good-good, which would explain it away.

revision.english: The father hastily put rice into the child's mouth.
Presently they laid down their chopsticks.
"Just a little longer," the man said firmly, as if to himself.
"Yes, let us work," she said, calmly and at peace. And holding the child upon her knees, she bared her small breast and began to give milk.
notes: Breast is literal; the Japanese has small nipple/breast put out for nursing.

revision.english: "Now, let us clear away. And let us sleep; let us get up early tomorrow."
Presently the man stood up. And when he was about to begin to clear the table, the child had already closed its eyes with its cheek against the breast. All about had fallen quite still.
"A storm," the man whispered, standing still.
notes: Kept the last line plain and short as the closing of the storm frame.

revision.english: The parents and child had gathered at the table under the dim electric light hanging close to the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. The father and the mother were both still truly young. And the child was a plump little girl, just able to stand by holding to the table.

"You won't listen, you." The young father gazed steadily at the small round arms and at her eyes with their rather dark, long lashes, darting nimbly and shrewdly without pause, as if at a loss what to do, and then with a smile over his whole face, pinching lightly with his finger the child's round, thrust-out cheek, he took a large tea-bowl as if groping for it from under the table and put it in her hand.

Standing unsteadily, the child was trying with fat, round hands, short as balls to stir everything on the table, leaving not a moment's gap, and far too fast. So, smiling, they put everything, the tea-bowls and the earthen teapot and the aluminium pot, under the table. On the table there remained only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.

The mother served the hot, freshly cooked rice, its white steam rising thick, from the pot and handed it to him. And her own young, large eyes, too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for a moment, lovely as a little bird. And as if unable to bear it, murmuring within her mouth, wondering whatever was the matter with this child, with a look of finding her so dear there was nothing to be done about it, she said strongly, "Bōya," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And as if having forgotten everything, the three smiled at one another as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle and with smile and gladness welling up of itself besides. And in the clatter and noise, they did not hear the sound of the wind and rain.

The young father kept his big red hand spread busily over the table. And his eyes, holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, as he steadied the child he put a little food into that small red mouth. In between, hastily opening his own big mouth, he pushed rice into it.

The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty between the teeth, as if it had frozen, and thoroughly nasty. As if startled, she said nothing and bit it again with her front teeth, but her heart had already, before she knew it, bowed down in loneliness.

And it seemed to her like a life that had gone on far too long. She found herself thinking, all at once, as if she had grown quite old. And her far heart quietly remembered days filled with quiet tears, and days threatened and spent in fear for material things, and each and every day grieved and suffered through sickness. Yet to her remembering now, all of it was like a dream. Suffering and sorrow, too, were like a fond dream.

It was in a dim, faint light, and, quiet like that light, three people were drawn together with their heads together telling a long story That story seemed to go on between them, so long and without ceasing. And in that story all seemed to be told, all the good and evil of the world, sorrow and suffering and anger and trouble, and joy, all of it. Yet those who spoke and those who listened only went on quietly and peacefully smiling, and they did not move at all. With their heads inclined and their eyes lowered, only quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to wrap them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.

The far picture was mirrored darkly and quietly in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely peace, that picture was to be seen. Young, she sighed a lonely, secret sigh by herself, and glanced at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and the child, and remained silent.

Yes. That day was there. The day when all would turn to fond remembrance and forgiveness and peace was there. After a long life, and after a long sorrow, and after a long suffering, on the day after all of that, that peaceful day of fond remembrance and forgiveness was there. What was the suffering or sorrow of each single day? What was the tiredness or trouble of each single day? Before she knew it she had a smile on her face.
"It is only three years, isn't it. And yet you and I have known a great deal of hardship."

crux.for_the_english: So: keep the trigger physical and uninterpreted. The potato is hard — “as if frozen”, gritty between her teeth, tasteless — and the distance it opens in her is rendered in the narration's ordinary diction of distance itself (“far”, “far off”, “far heart”, “rate”, repeated until it becomes a place). Do not name what she sees: not heaven, not death, not her own old age, not a judgement day, though it has something of all of them. “あの日” is only “that day”. The picture must stay a picture — 幻のような絵, “a picture like a phantom”, something her eye sees, not a doctrine she arrives at. An English version that upgrades the vision into consolation — that lets her (or the narrator) conclude anything — has written a religious tract over a story about a bad potato. Likewise keep the return unexalted: “もう少しの間だ” — “just a little longer” — nursing the child, clearing the table, getting up early tomorrow. The vision does not solve the poverty. It sits next to it, and the story ends not on it but on a man standing still, whispering, 「嵐だな」 — “a storm”. That bare last line is the frame closing: the storm announced in p1, unheard through the child's noise in p8, heard by her alone inside her silence in p19, and finally heard by everyone in the quiet of p37–38. Keep it exactly that plain and that short; do not let it swell into a symbol at the last moment.
crux.point: "The crux is the mother's mid-mouthful slide out of time. For five paragraphs this is a warm, crowded, slightly comic supper: a fat baby girl just able to stand by holding the table, banging a spoon, everything swept out of her reach, two young parents — not a wrinkle on either face, but a deep, drowsy tiredness already in his hollowed eyes and her fine shoulders — laughing helplessly and forgetting, in the racket, even to hear the storm outside. Then, in p10–p11, the mother puts a potato in her mouth. It is hard, gritty, as if frozen, thoroughly nasty. She says nothing. And the prose, without any marker of a scene-change, drifts with her: the three years since her marriage stretch until she feels she has lived a whole long life and grown quite old; the sufferings of those three years come back “dreamlike”, and she is suddenly seeing, from very far away, a dim picture (絵) of three people with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, joy — is told, while nobody moves, nobody is disturbed, and all of it is wrapped in 懐かしみ (natsukashimi, fond remembrance) and 許し (forgiveness) and a deep peace like the night's. The story stands or falls on whether the English lets that expansion happen inside an ordinary sentence at an ordinary table, and then lets it contract again to “only three years” (p14, p22, p27) and to work tomorrow."

The child's noise in the first movement is not decoration — it is what the world sounds like from inside a life being lived at full stretch, and the mother's silence in the second half is set against her husband's repeated, puzzled 「どうして黙ってるの」 (“why are you so quiet?”, p19, p21) precisely because he cannot follow her where she has gone. And the vision's content is all summary and no event: nothing is shown happening, only everything having already happened and turned, in the telling, into fondness and pardon. crux.for_the_english: Do not label it — not 'she imagined heaven', 'she dreamed', 'she thought of death'. Keep the modal, unresolved terms ('that day', 'would', 'seemed', 'as if'), let the vision arrive and recede unexplained, and keep it visually still rather than turning it into narrative action.
crux.point: The bad potato turns an ordinary supper into life seen from beyond its end, and that vision must stay unexplained.
crux.why: Nothing dramatic happens: in p11–13 the potato is inexplicably hard, 'frozen', tasteless, and its 'unconnected cold badness' detaches the young mother from the room. She feels suddenly old, remembers the three married years as if from far away — suffering already 'like a dream' (p13) — then sees, p16–18, three motionless figures in dim light telling an endless story in which good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy are all spoken of, yet wrapped only in 'nostalgia and forgiveness' and deep rest, 'like night'. In p20 she repeats the turn as certainty: 'that day exists', after long life, long sorrow. The story stands on this not being reduced to a cause: not simply fatigue, not a stated premonition of death, not religious consolation, not a daydream about old age. It is the present moment already viewed from after time has passed over it (p17: life will pass, and only on that passed day does everything change to nostalgia and forgiveness).

crux.for_the_english: Resist rationalisation, expansion and synonym-variation (Berman's tidyings). Keep long cumulative sentences where the Japanese accumulates, repeat the same English words for the same Japanese ones — quiet, lonely, far, rest/peace, nostalgic/dear, smile, dream — even where elegant English would vary them, and keep dialogue plain and slightly unfinished ('It's only been... hasn't it', 'just a little longer').
crux.point: The incantatory repetition and unbroken domestic surface are how three years become a lifetime; varied, tightened prose would make the vision an inserted purple passage instead of a change of distance.
crux.why: The text works by recurrence, not event: storm heard at start, forgotten in the child's noise (p8, p19, p38), people repeatedly 'young' yet exhausted (p2–3 against p13–14: barely three years, yet she feels wholly aged), words circling — 静か, 淋しい, 遠い, 安らかさ, なつかしみ, 許し, 微笑, 夢 — across both the noisy supper and the silent vision, so the vision feels like the same room seen from far off rather than another world. Sentences also drift: dropped subjects, tense loosening, だろう / やうだ speculation, and dialogue that resolves nothing except 'let us work', 'clear up', 'get up early tomorrow' (p34–36).

payload.english: Outside the door, darkened before they knew it, there was the sound of hard wind and rain. A storm.

The parent and child had gathered at the table under the dim electric light hanging close to the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. The father and the mother were both still truly young. And the child was a plump little girl, just able to stand by holding to the table.
notes: くりくりと肥ってる: kuri-kuri suggests roundness and plumpness rather than curly hair; rendered as plump to keep the bodily comedy plain.

payload.english: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kindly eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was to be seen a weary colour of tiredness. And in the colour of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was to be seen a still deeper, sunken tiredness, and a drowsy peace.
The day had ended. The sorrow and the suffering of that day were about to flow into the peace of the night. And they smiled in silence and fixed their eyes on all of the child.
notes: その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ kept as all of the child to preserve the subete repetition rather than smoothing to everything about her.

So, smiling, they put everything, the tea-bowls and the earthen teapot and the aluminium pot, under the table. On the table there remained only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
notes: Tableware kept plain as poverty-modernity detail without gloss; smiling repeats the hohoemi chain.

payload.english: She served the hot, freshly cooked rice, with its white steam rising thick, from the pot and handed it to him. And her own young, large eyes, too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for a moment, lovely as a little bird. And as if unable to bear it, murmuring within her mouth, wondering whatever was the matter with this child, with a look of finding her so dear there was nothing to be done about it, she said firmly, "Bōya," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And as if having forgotten everything, the three smiled at one another as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle and with the smile and gladness welling up of itself on top of it. And in the clatter and noise, they did not hear the sound of the wind and rain.
notes: I keep Bōya in roman letters for 坊や: the child has been stated to be a girl, but the mother calls to her with this affectionate address. 'Boy' or a name would mislead.

payload.english: The mother, silent with bowed head close by the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onion, the carrot and potato stewed in the deep blue pot. And about to say something, she put into her mouth a potato stewed sweet and soft, and looked at the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and gazed vacantly at a far place.

The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty between the teeth, as if it had frozen, and thoroughly nasty. As if startled, she said nothing and bit it again with her front teeth, but her heart had already, before she knew it, bowed down lonely.

payload.english: She recalled the suffering and sorrow and tiredness of each day. And the tasteless, indifferent, cold nastiness of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow-filled, real life since her marriage.
notes: Kept 'far-removed heart' literal as the ordinary diction of distance that carries the slide.

payload.english: And it seemed to her like a life that had gone on far too long. She found herself thinking, all at once, as if she had grown quite old. And of days filled with quiet tears, and of days threatened and spent in fear for material things, and of each and every day grieved and suffered through sickness, her far heart was quietly remembering. Yet to her remembering now, all of it was like a dream. Suffering and sorrow, too, were like a fond dream.
notes: 'For material things' keeps busshitsu literal; I take it as want and money pressure but did not replace it. 'Fond dream' keeps natsukashii in plain English, ahead of the natsukashimi trio, without turning it into nostalgia.

payload.english: And when she thought, it was no more than barely three years of life since her marriage.
She gazed vacantly far off, as if her attention had been caught by something before she knew it. Her quiet heart was, before she knew it, seeing a picture like a phantom.
notes: Kept e as 'picture' and maboroshi no you na as 'like a phantom', not vision or dream, so it stays something seen by the eye.

payload.english: It was in a dim, faint light, and, quiet like that light, three people drawing together with their heads together telling a long story. That story seemed to go on between them, so long and without ceasing. And in that story all seemed to be told, all the good and evil of the world, sorrow and suffering and anger and anguish, and joy, all of it. Yet those who spoke and those who listened only went on quietly and peacefully smiling, and they did not move at all. With their heads inclined and their eyes lowered, only quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to wrap them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
notes: Kept the three people unidentified and the picture a picture: no heaven, death or judgement added. Chose plain 'fond remembrance' for natsukashimi and 'forgiveness' for yurushi, and kept smile, all, long and quiet repeated as in the Japanese.

payload.english: All things of the world, a life, would pass. And only on that day, when it had passed, would all, all things, turn to fond remembrance and forgiveness. And at that time they would be before a rest like night, forever.

notes: Kept 'far', 'eyes', 'lonely' and 'quiet' repeated as distance-words, and 'remained silent' to hold the silence against the earlier noise.

hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is hard, gritty/crunchy (ざくざく), as if frozen, tasteless/nasty (不味). Period poor-cooking/storage detail. Keep physical and uninterpreted; do not make it symbolize poverty or turn causality explicit (potato = vision). English must keep teeth, coldness, lack of taste without ennobling or explaining.

幻のような絵, 淡暗い光り, 物静か — picture stays a picture seen by the eye, not a dream entered or doctrine concluded. Do not translate 絵 as vision/scene/world, 幻 as hallucination/dream, or upgrade dimness into mysticism.

懐かしみ (natsukashimi), 許し, 安らかさ, 安息 — repeated network. Natsukashimi is fond remembrance/longing, not nostalgia in modern English sense and not forgiveness; 許し is pardon/forgiveness. Keep same English words each time; do not expand into explanations or merge them.

あの日, 永久に夜のような安息 — that day / night-like rest. Could imply death, old age, eternity, judgement. Text leaves open. Keep literal 'that day' and 'rest like night'; do not name heaven, death, afterlife, or judgement day.

Child explicitly girl but called 坊や (Bōya, literally boy). Period affectionate generic for baby. Keep 'Bōya' (romanised, explained in margin once) rather than 'boy/son/little one' which either misgenders or erases the wrinkle, and do not invent a name.

卓《テーブル》, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》 — Taishō literary with old kana and ruby glosses. Table is Western-style table under bare bulb; aluminium pot, earthen teapot, beef/onion/carrot/potato mark pauvre modernity. Render plainly without exoticizing or modernizing; ruby shows reading, not emphasis.

motifs.why: Second half is defined by mother's silence against first-half racket; husband's repeated question marks it.

motifs.english: Keep 'tiredness / weary' for 疲れ/だるそう/打沈んだ. Physical, shared, young yet exhausted; do not pathologize.
motifs.why: Establishes poverty of strength without wrinkles; motivates but does not explain vision.

motifs.english: Keep fixed trio: 'fond remembrance (natsukashimi) and forgiveness and peace'. Gloss natsukashimi once in margin; thereafter same words. 'That day' stays 'that day'.
motifs.motif: fond remembrance, forgiveness, peace / night-like rest
motifs.why: Vision's whole content is these nouns; any elegant variation turns summary into doctrine.

motifs.english: Keep wife's exact refrain 'only three years / barely three years' (p14, p22, p27) and husband's echo 'only two years past' (p25, p28). Do not improve her inarticulacy.
motifs.motif: only three years; just a little longer; let's work
motifs.why: Contraction back to ordinary time and unexalted endurance; mother's eloquence must stay limited to this.

narration.english_tense: Simple past throughout as default. Keep explanatory past (it was, it was that) for p2-p4 scene-setting and for gnomic vision summary p17; do not switch vision to present timeless or dialogue to present.
narration.frame: One supper in a small room under a dark bulb, storm outside. Narration begins external and comic-crowded, drifts with mother without scene-break, contracts to table-clearing and whispered storm.
narration.narrator: Third-person external narrator, initially distanced (親子, 男, 女), imperceptibly becoming mother's interior focalization from p10-p11 onward. No italics, no dream-marking, no psychologizing verbs; hedges (いつか, ふと, いつとなく, なにか, ように) and explanatory endings (であった, のであった, のだった) keep reverie in same grammar as table.
narration.tense_habits: Japanese past/explanatory (であった, のであった, のだった) for both outer fact and inner summary; progressive/distal forms (〜しつつ, 〜ようとしてゐる, 〜てゐた) for ongoing supper vs completed drift. Hedged perception verbs, not marked thought.
timeline: p1-p9: crowded comic supper — baby stands holding table, bangs spoon, parents sweep everything below table, forget storm in racket
p10-p11: trigger — mother serves beef/onion/carrot/potato from blue pot, tastes hard gritty tasteless potato, falls vaguely silent
p12-p18: expansion — three married years feel lifelong, sufferings recalled dreamlike, phantom-like picture of three telling endless story, night-like rest ahead
p19-p32: return punctured by dialogue — husband twice 'why are you silent?', wife can only say 'only three years', husband answers 'two years past, baby will walk, a little longer', feeding resumes
p33-p38: close — chopsticks laid down, nursing, clear table sleep early tomorrow, child asleep at breast, stillness, husband stands whispering storm

bible.say: This bible keeps the supper crowded and the vision dim: repeat smile, eyes, far, all, long, quiet, tiredness, and the fixed trio of fond remembrance/forgiveness/peace in plain past-tense English, leave that day and the three figures unidentified, leave Bōya as Bōya, and let the storm frame open and shut without swelling.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse; margin only where sentence cannot give reader the thing: Bōya (affectionate address for baby despite girl child), aluminium pot / beef-pot supper as poverty-modernity, 懐かしみ gloss once, old-kana ruby convention. Never annotate what context supplies or explain that day.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taishō literary but not quaint: soft, slightly formal, accumulative long sentences with repetitions, then short dialogue punctures. Keep drift in same diction as table; no italics for thought, no vividness upgrade for vision, no sentimentality for baby, no consolation conclusion. Husband's practical hope stands equal to vision.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No personal names in text. Use 'the man / the young father', 'the woman / the mother', 'the child / the baby' as Japanese does; do not normalize to husband/wife/father/mother throughout. Keep 'Bōya' for 坊や as address with one margin note; do not translate to boy/son/baby.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Bōya only, in romanisation with macron-less plain form. All else in English: Sensei-type retention does not apply (no 先生). Foods, vessels (rice, aluminium pot, earthen teapot, tea-bowl) in plain English.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for direct speech and ひとりで独言. In English use double quotation marks for spoken lines (p7, p21-p35, p38 whisper). Husband's どうして黙ってるの twice must read as same question. Do not join dialogue to narration or split drift sentences to make logic clearer.
style_sheet.register: Clean, soft, slightly formal past-tense English. Poverty plain without ennoblement; comedy bodily without cuteness; abstraction flat without elegance. Repeat words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese varies.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby in source (卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》) shows reading; render as normal English ('table', 'shrewd', 'smile') with no italics. No italics for vision or thought. Italics only for Bōya as foreign address on first use if house style requires, then roman.

底本：「素木しづ作品集」札幌・北書房
　　　1970（昭和45）年6月15日発行
底本の親本：「文章倶楽部」

入力：小林徹
校正：湯地光弘
1999年9月5日公開
2005年12月29日修正
青空文庫作成ファイル：
このファイルは、インターネットの図書館、青空文庫（http://www.aozora.gr.jp/）で作られました。入力、校正、制作にあたったのは、ボランティアの皆さんです。

crux.for_the_english: So: keep the trigger physical and uninterpreted. The potato is hard — “as if frozen”, gritty between her teeth, tasteless — and the distance it opens in her is rendered in the narration's ordinary diction of distance itself (“far”, “far off”, “far heart”, “rate”, repeated until it becomes a place). Do not name what she sees: not heaven, not death, not her own old age, not a judgement day, though it has something of all of them. “あの日” is only “that day”. The picture must stay a picture — 幻のような絵, “a picture like a phantom”, something her eye sees, not a doctrine she arrives at. An English version that upgrades the vision into consolation — that lets her (or the narrator) conclude anything — has written a religious tract over a story about a bad potato. Likewise keep the return unexalted: “もう少しの間だ” — “just a little longer” — nursing the child, clearing the table, getting up early tomorrow. The vision does not solve the poverty. It sits next to it, and the story ends not on it but on a man standing still, whispering, 「嵐だな」 — “a storm”. That bare last line is the frame closing: the storm announced in p1, unheard through the child's noise in p8, heard by her alone inside her silence in p19, and finally heard by everyone in the quiet of p37–38. Keep it exactly that plain and that short; do not let it swell into a symbol at the last moment.
crux.point: "The crux is the mother's mid-mouthful slide out of time. For five paragraphs this is a warm, crowded, slightly comic supper: a fat baby girl just able to stand by holding the table, banging a spoon, everything swept out of her reach, two young parents — not a wrinkle on either face, but a deep, drowsy tiredness already in his hollowed eyes and her fine shoulders — laughing helplessly and forgetting, in the racket, even to hear the storm outside. Then, in p10–p11, the mother puts a potato in her mouth. It is hard, gritty, as if frozen, thoroughly nasty. She says nothing. And the prose, without any marker of a scene-change, drifts with her: the three years since her marriage stretch until she feels she has lived a whole long life and grown quite old; the sufferings of those three years come back “dreamlike”, and she is suddenly seeing, from very far away, a dim picture (絵) of three people with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, joy — is told, while nobody moves, nobody is disturbed, and all of it is wrapped in 懐かしみ (natsukashimi, fond remembrance) and 許し (forgiveness) and a deep peace like the night's. The story stands or falls on whether the English lets that expansion happen inside an ordinary sentence at an ordinary table, and then lets it contract again to “only three years” (p14, p22, p27) and to work tomorrow."
crux.why: Everything else in the text serves that one movement. The frame is built for it: storm heard / storm unheard / storm heard again. The child's noise in the first movement is not decoration — it is what the world sounds like from inside a life being lived at full stretch, and the mother's silence in the second half is set against her husband's repeated, puzzled 「どうして黙ってるの」 (“why are you so quiet?”, p19, p21) precisely because he cannot follow her where she has gone. And the vision's content is all summary and no event: nothing is shown happening, only everything having already happened and turned, in the telling, into fondness and pardon. If the English makes the vision vivid, specific or dramatic, the ratio inverts and it becomes a fantasy interrupting a domestic sketch, rather than the domestic sketch briefly seen from the far side of a whole life.

open_questions.question: Who are the three people in dim picture? Family aged, themselves in afterlife, humanity generic? Text keeps three quiet people, heads together. Don't identify.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If identified as family in old age/heaven, vision becomes specific consolation and loses universality/ambiguity.

open_questions.question: "That day" when all becomes nostalgia/forgiveness - death, old age, far future, eternity before night-like rest? Keep literal that day/night-like rest unresolved.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Naming death/heaven clarifies author's deliberate vagueness and changes theology/tone.

open_questions.question: Baby explicitly girl in p2, yet parents call her Bōya (boy/baby lad). Keep Bōya as affectionate generic 'baby/little one' without correcting gender or inventing name?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Correcting to 'little girl' erases period colloquial address; transliterating unexplained confuses.

open_questions.question: Potato: frozen-like hard gritty undercooked potato - literal poor cooking/storage period detail, not metaphor invented. Keep texture words close.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Symbolising potato destroys crux trigger's ordinariness.

reading.reading: The crux must stay first in drafting. Beyond it, notice the narration's slide: begins outside ('a parent and child', 'the man', 'the woman') and imperceptibly becomes the mother's interior in same past-tense explanatory endings (de atta / no datta) and same 'as if', 'somehow', 'before she knew it' hedges. No italics, dreams marked, or psychologising verbs should separate reverie. Long sentences accumulate repetitions - smile (hohoemi), eyes/gaze, quiet/still, dream, all/everything (subete), long (nagai), far - then dialogue punctures with short exchanges. Repeat English words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese does. Register Taishō literary with old kana but not quaint: clean, soft, slightly formal English, poverty plain (rice, aluminium pot, beef onion carrot potato) without ennobling supper. Parents unnamed, young yet exhausted; child noisy bodily comedy prevents sentimentality. Husband's practical hope ('little one will soon walk', 'let's work') not lesser than vision. Fluent risks: rationalising potato-to-vision causality, clarifying 'that day', expanding abstract nouns into explanations, destroying rhythm by splitting drift or joining dialogue, impoverishing subete/nagai/far repetitions, making mother eloquent - she can say almost nothing, repeatedly 'only three years', and husband misunderstands kindly.
reading.say: I can't settle identity of three figures or nature of that day from text; that's intentional ambiguity, not gap to fill. Also Bōya for girl child likely generic affectionate address in period, but keep visible as choice/fork.

voice_takes.label: Quiet drift (recommended)
voice_takes.line: "叙述は温かい同室の声から、区切りなく母の遠い心へ滑る" — narration slides without break from warm room to mother's far heart. Clean slightly formal prose, long looping sentences, repeated plain words; parents young plainspoken, husband blunt warm ('sa da naa' as soft 'that's so'), mother halting almost monosyllabic; wrong: lyrical uplift, heaven language, modern therapy idiom, cute baby-talk.

voice_takes.label: Plainer and drier
voice_takes.line: Shorter English sentences, abstract nouns kept bare (fondness, forgiveness, peace) without softening, dialogue working-plain. Risk: vision reads stark/fatalistic rather than tender.

voice_takes.label: Slightly period-formal
voice_takes.line: More formal diction and slower cadence matching 1917 literary surface, parents courteous-distanced. Risk: archaism makes poverty picturesque and mother remote, wrong if it sounds translated-old rather than young.

release.title: 晩餐

casual.en: Outside the door, darkened before they knew it, there was the sound of hard wind and rain. A storm.
casual.ja: いつか暗くなった戸の外に、激しい雨風の音がする、嵐だ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The parents and child had gathered at the table under the dim electric light hanging close to the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. The father and the mother were both still truly young. And the child was a plump little girl, just able to stand by holding to the table.
casual.ja: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。まだ本当に父も母も若かった。そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the man's hollowed, kindly eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was to be seen a weary colour of tiredness. And in the colour of the woman's dark hair and about her slender shoulders there was to be seen a still deeper, sunken tiredness, and a drowsy peace.
casual.ja: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The day had ended. The sorrow and the suffering of that day were about to flow into the peace of the night. And they smiled in silence and fixed their eyes on all of the child.
casual.ja: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Standing unsteadily, the child was trying with fat, round hands, short as balls to stir everything on the table, leaving not a moment's gap, and far too fast. So, smiling, they put everything, the tea-bowls and the earthen teapot and the aluminium pot, under the table. On the table there remained only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
casual.ja: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: But the child gave a noisy cry full of small joy and banged the spoon and the plate down upon the table.
casual.ja: けれども子供は、さわがしい、小さなよろこびに満ちた叫声を上げて、スプーンと皿をテーブルの上にたゝきつけた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "You won't listen, you." The young father gazed steadily at the small round arms and at her eyes with their rather dark, long lashes, darting nimbly and shrewdly without pause, as if at a loss what to do, and then with a smile over his whole face, pinching lightly with his finger the child's round, thrust-out cheek, he took a large tea-bowl as if groping for it from under the table and put it in her hand.
casual.ja: 『きかない奴だな。』若い父親は、その小さなまるい腕や、敏捷に怜悧にすきもなく動いてる、黒みがちの睫のながい子供の瞳をぢっと見てゐると、どうしたらいゝだらうといふやうに、やがて顔一ぱいな微笑を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら、大きな茶碗をテーブルの下から探すやうにしてとると、彼女の手に渡した。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The mother served the hot, freshly cooked rice, its white steam rising thick, from the pot and handed it to him. And her own young, large eyes, too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for a moment, lovely as a little bird. And as if unable to bear it, murmuring within her mouth, wondering whatever was the matter with this child, with a look of finding her so dear there was nothing to be done about it, she said strongly, "Bōya," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And as if having forgotten everything, the three smiled at one another as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle and with smile and gladness welling up of itself besides. And in the clatter and noise, they did not hear the sound of the wind and rain.
casual.ja: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: Bōya is an affectionate way of addressing a very small child, though literally it suggests a boy; the child here has been introduced as a little girl.

casual.en: The young father kept his big red hand spread busily over the table. And his eyes, holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, as he steadied the child he put a little food into that small red mouth. In between, hastily opening his own big mouth, he pushed rice into it.
casual.ja: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The mother, silent with bowed head close by the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onion, the carrot and potato stewed in the deep blue pot. And about to say something, she put into her mouth a potato stewed sweet and soft, and looked at the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and gazed vacantly at a far place.
casual.ja: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty between the teeth, as if it had frozen, and thoroughly nasty. As if startled, she said nothing and bit it again with her front teeth, but her heart had already, before she knew it, bowed down in loneliness.
casual.ja: 彼女の口のなかのジャガ芋が、丁度凍ったかのやうに固くざく〳〵してゐて、非常に不味かったのだった。彼女はふと驚いたやうに黙って前歯でかみなほしたが、彼女の心は、いつか淋しくうつむいてしまってゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: She recalled the suffering and sorrow and tiredness of each day. And the tasteless, indifferent, cold nastiness of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow-filled, real life since her marriage.
casual.ja: 彼女は日々の苦しみや悲しみ疲れを思出したのであった。そしてジャガ芋の無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さが、彼女に静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心を与へた。彼女は結婚後の貧しい悲しみにみちた現実の生活を思ひ浮べたのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: And it seemed to her like a life that had gone on far too long. She found herself thinking, all at once, as if she had grown quite old. And her far heart quietly remembered days filled with quiet tears, and days threatened and spent in fear for material things, and each and every day grieved and suffered through sickness. Yet to her remembering now, all of it was like a dream. Suffering and sorrow, too, were like a fond dream.
casual.ja: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: And when she thought, it was no more than barely three years of life since her marriage.
casual.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: She gazed vacantly far off, as if her attention had been caught by something before she knew it. Her quiet heart was, before she knew it, seeing a picture like a phantom.
casual.ja: 彼女は、いつとなく何物にか気をとられたやうに、ぼんやりと遠くの方を見てゐた。彼女のその静かな心が、いつか幻のやうな絵を見てゐたのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: It was in a dim, faint light, and, quiet like that light, three people were drawn together with their heads together telling a long story. That story seemed to go on between them, so long and without ceasing. And in that story all seemed to be told, all the good and evil of the world, sorrow and suffering and anger and trouble, and joy, all of it. Yet those who spoke and those who listened only went on quietly and peacefully smiling, and they did not move at all. With their heads inclined and their eyes lowered, only quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to wrap them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
casual.ja: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: All things of the world, a life, would pass. And only on that day, when it had passed, would all, all things, turn to fond remembrance and forgiveness. And at that time they would be before a rest like night, forever.
casual.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The far picture was mirrored darkly and quietly in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely peace, that picture was to be seen. Young, she sighed a lonely, secret sigh by herself, and glanced at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and the child, and remained silent.
casual.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Why are you so quiet?" the man said, looking at the woman's face in puzzlement. curious.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。

curious.en: "Yes, let us work," she said, calmly and at peace. And holding the child upon her knees, she bared her small nipple and began to suckle her.
curious.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Now, let us clear away. And let us sleep; let us get up early tomorrow."
curious.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Presently the man stood up. And when he was about to begin to clear the table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All around had fallen quite still.

curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "A storm," the man whispered, standing still.
